title: Blink and the Day Is Gone!
displayName: Week 5 Tuesday Blink and the Day Is Gone!

source.pdf: 初2第3辑初中时文阅读提分训练3+X第3辑8年级.pdf

content.v: Have you ever felt a day pass by super quickly? Last summer, it really did! In July and August 2025, scientists recorded several of the fastest days in recent history. On these days, the Earth spun a tiny bit faster than normal—about one thousandth of a second faster.
We all know a day is 24 hours long. That’s 1,440 minutes, or 86,400 seconds. That’s how long it usually takes the Earth to
spin
around once. But that’s only an
average
. In reality, the Earth’s spin changes slightly every day. Sometimes it’s slower. Sometimes, like last summer, it’s faster.
For thousands of years, people used the Earth’s spin to tell time. But in the 1950s, scientists began using atomic clocks. These clocks are based on how fast atoms
vibrate
. They are so
accurate
that they can measure tiny changes in the Earth’s speed—just a few
milliseconds
. That is far quicker than the blink of an eye!

In July 2024, the fastest day ever was recorded. The Earth finished its spin about 1.65 milliseconds early. July 9 and August 5, 2025, were also “fast days”. On each, the Earth turned about 1.3 milliseconds faster than usual.
What makes our planet speed up or slow down? The Moon’s gravity plays a big role. As the Moon
orbits
the Earth, sometimes it’s closer, and sometimes it’s farther away. And the Moon’s
orbit

itself doesn’t stay fixed—it moves in space. Other factors, such as the Earth’s atmosphere and major wind systems, can also affect the Earth’s spin. It may be surprising that the Earth’s core, deep inside our planet, can affect its speed as well.

Even though we’ve had some fast days recently, scientists say that over millions of years, Earth is actually slowing down. It loses a couple of milliseconds every hundred years. So, if you feel like time is flying, enjoy it—our planet won’t keep up this pace forever.
